sentence: A company can run one AI model in several places, called deployments, that share one public model name [RSELECT-001].
For each request, this part of the router finds every deployment that could serve that name [RSELECT-020].
Filters can then drop deployments that are unhealthy, resting after recent errors, paused, or reserved for another team [RSELECT-024], [RSELECT-043], [RSELECT-044], [RSELECT-046].
By default the router picks one of the rest at random [RSELECT-067], [RSELECT-139].
When the filters leave none, the caller usually gets an error with status 429, which here means no deployment could take the request [RSELECT-054], [RSELECT-283].
On the full path, the router also writes this failure to its info log [RSELECT-054].
One wrong setting can fail every request for a model [RSELECT-279].
An asynchronous call runs the full path only when the router-wide strategy is one of the five full-path strategies [RSELECT-060].
A routing group's or request's own strategy does not count, and synchronous calls always take the reduced path [RSELECT-060], [RSELECT-121].
The full path starts with the pre-routing hook, where a strategy router can move the request to one of its tiers [RSELECT-061].
Common resolution then turns the name into candidates, and a fixed sequence of filters narrows them [RSELECT-020], [RSELECT-040].
The strategy picks one survivor [RSELECT-067], [RSELECT-068].
An empty list raises `RouterRateLimitError` with status 429 [RSELECT-054].
model group: the public model name a request asks for; several deployments can share it
deployment: one place a model runs, with its own provider model, credentials and limits
asynchronous call: a request through the router's asynchronous methods, such as its async chat call; it starts at the async entry point
synchronous call: a request whose selection runs synchronously, such as sync image generation; it always takes the reduced path
full path: the whole selection: pre-routing hook, name lookup, every filter, then the pick
reduced path: selection without the pre-routing hook, team and web-search filters, callback checks or tag routing, which a router with routing plugins refuses
router-wide strategy: the strategy setting of the whole router; it alone decides between the full and reduced paths, while a routing group's or request's own strategy changes only the final pick
five full-path strategies: simple-shuffle (the default), least-busy, latency-based-routing, cost-based-routing and usage-based-routing-v2
other strategy names: the three other accepted names, usage-based-routing, lar1 and provider-budget-routing; any other name is rejected
routing group: a named set of model groups sharing one strategy; a request can name the group itself unless a model or alias already uses that name
pre-routing hook: the first step of the full path, where a strategy router can move the request to one of its tiers
strategy router: an entry under a model name that never calls a provider; it sends the request to one of its tiers, other model names, chosen by its own logic
tag filtering: a switch, for the router or for one request, that lets request tags narrow which deployments serve it
tier params: settings a strategy router pins for its chosen tier, such as an output-token limit or a reasoning effort
session binding: for Claude Code command-line traffic only: a one-hour link, renewed on use, that sends a session's child-agent requests through the strategy router its main requests used
common resolution: the name lookup that turns the requested name into candidates
specific-deployment request: a request option that matches deployments by provider model string, such as openai/gpt-4o, instead of by model name
provider model: the provider's own model string that a deployment calls, such as openai/gpt-4o
deployment id: the unique name of one deployment, such as dep-0
alias: a second name that points at a model group, followed one hop
wildcard route: a deployment registered under a name pattern, such as openai/*-mini, that serves any name the pattern matches from its start
team filter: usually keeps deployments with no owner team plus the caller's team's; an admin without a team reaches one team's deployments, but a name two teams share is refused
note: TARGETS-100: the filter 'keeps deployments with no owner team ... plus those owned by the request's team'; with no team id every team-owned deployment is lost. TARGETS-103: a proxy admin with no team id, when every candidate is team-owned and named exactly the requested model, gets the candidates 'returned unfiltered when they all belong to one team'. TARGETS-104: from more than one team it 'raises BadRequestError (status 400)' saying the name 'matches deployments from multiple teams'. RSELECT-041 names this proxy-admin disambiguation as step 2. The code agrees (common_utils.py filter_team_based_models). RSELECT-013/014 add that the lookup raises the same error when it gathers every team's deployments under a public name, which fits the sentence. The row leaves out the narrow condition that the name's candidates must all be team-owned (with a public deployment of the same name the admin gets only the public one, no refusal); that is below glossary grain and 'usually' frames the row. 'Refused' fits a 400.

sentence: web-search filter: for a request that asks for a web-search tool, keeps deployments not marked as lacking web search
access-group filter: the lookup step that checks the caller's key against access groups and can narrow the candidates to deployments in groups the key allows
reservation filter: drops strategy routers, then deployments that an access window or a provisioned-throughput share keeps for other teams
access window: daily hours, in a set timezone, when a deployment serves only listed teams
provisioned-throughput share: a team's slice of a shared provisioned deployment; a team holding one uses only its shared deployments, and teams without one are kept off them
generic fallback list: the fallbacks entry under a literal star key; lookup uses its first name for an unmatched name, and the list can also be the chain after a failed call
health-check routing: a switch that lets background health checks remove unhealthy deployments
allowed-failures policy: per-error-type counts of failures a deployment may have before it cools down
cooldown: a pause after recent errors during which selection skips a deployment, 5 seconds unless the router sets another length; the failure-handling chapter covers it
paused deployment: a deployment whose blocked setting is the value true itself; the text "true" does not count
callback checks: optional extra filters, such as rate limits, affinity, prompt caching and stream continuation
affinity: keeping a caller, a session or an earlier response on the deployment that already served it
pre-call checks: the router's own tests of each deployment's context window, per-minute request count and region, plus one request setting
structured-output setting: the request's response format, the only request setting that pre-call checks test for provider support
routing plugins: configured functions that can narrow which provider models may serve a request
order: a deployment's priority number; selection keeps the lowest number present, and a higher number serves when the request names that level, as an order fallback does
exclusion lists: deployment ids that failover or a retry asks selection to skip
no-deployment error: the error raised when no candidate survives; it uses status 429 (too many requests), which here means no deployment could take the request
selection errors: the other errors: 400 for a bad name or a reservation, 503 for a paused deployment asked for by id, and errors when pre-call checks or routing plugins leave none
pass-through flag: marks a deployment that may serve pass-through endpoints, which use only marked deployments
selection trace: the trace span an asynchronous selection runs in, named route followed by the requested model
failure handlers: the request's logging handlers, which receive a full-path selection error when the request carries a logging object
settings update: the call that changes router settings while the router runs, and its companion that reads them; the next request uses a change
cache flush: a router call, also run by the router's reset call, that empties its caches; it is not a setting
Several deployments survive under the default `simple-shuffle`: a random pick, weighted by weight, rpm or tpm when set, else uniform
The filters leave nothing: `RouterRateLimitError` (429); the all-in-cooldown sentence appears only when every deployment id of the group is cooling
The cooldown filter empties the list, health-check routing is on and `allowed_fails_policy` is set: a warning, and the resting deployments stay candidates
The name is a deployment id, not a model name: that deployment after the reservation filter, with no health, cooldown, pre-call or tag filtering; if paused, `ServiceUnavailableError` (503)
A model group's only deployment is paused: the paused filter empties the list, so `RouterRateLimitError` (429), never the 503
Nothing matches, access groups emptied nothing, and a `"*"` list in `fallbacks` is non-empty: its first name serves the request, if that name resolves as a registered name

Nothing matches and no substitute resolves: `BadRequestError` (400) with an empty provider, naming the substitute if one was tried, else the requested name after its alias hop; configured fallbacks can still run
The router-wide strategy is not one of the five full-path strategies: an asynchronous call takes the reduced path
Routing plugins are configured and the call reaches the reduced path, or plugins narrow the list to nothing: `ValueError`; plugin narrowing never falls back to the unfiltered pool

Pre-call checks exclude every candidate, none for context window, and every group deployment would reject a non-string `response_format` sent while global drop-params is exactly off: `UnsupportedParamsError` (400)

Pre-call checks exclude every candidate, the row above does not apply, and one went for its rpm, which never happens under a router-wide `usage-based-routing-v2`: `RouterRateLimitErrorBasic` (429), even if others failed on context window
Pre-call checks exclude every candidate, some for context window and none for rpm: `ContextWindowExceededError`
Async pass-through selection ends with no deployment that sets `use_in_pass_through`: `BadRequestError`, even when only cooldown or health filters removed them
Selection has a full path and a reduced path that skips several checks [RSELECT-060], [RSELECT-128].
An asynchronous call takes the full path only when the router-wide strategy is one of the five full-path strategies, and a synchronous call always takes the reduced path [RSELECT-060], [RSELECT-121].

The calling method decides first: An asynchronous call, such as the async chat call, starts at the full-path check [RCALL-045], [RSELECT-060]. Asynchronous pass-through selection skips this check and always runs the pre-routing hook [RSELECT-130]. Synchronous selection, such as sync image generation, always takes the reduced path [RCALL-106], [RSELECT-121].

Five strategies keep the full path: They are simple-shuffle, the default, plus least-busy, latency-based-routing, cost-based-routing and usage-based-routing-v2 [RSELECT-060], [RSELECT-139]. The other accepted names, usage-based-routing, lar1 and provider-budget-routing, take the reduced path [RSELECT-060], [CONTRACTS-116].

A group's own strategy does not count: Only the router-wide strategy counts here [RSELECT-060]. A routing group or one request can name its own strategy, which changes only how the final pick is made [RSELECT-063], [RSELECT-278].

What the reduced path skips: It skips the pre-routing hook, the team and web-search filters, callback checks and tag routing [RSELECT-128]. It never runs routing plugins, so on a router that has them every reduced-path call fails before any lookup [RSELECT-128], [RSELECT-120].
Plugins refuse the reduced path: A router with routing plugins fails the call before any lookup rather than skip its plugins [RSELECT-120].
The check compares only the router-wide `routing_strategy` with the five full-path strategies [RSELECT-060].
With routing plugins configured, the reduced path raises `ValueError`, even for an asynchronous call handed down to it [RSELECT-120].
Some model names belong to a strategy router, which never calls a provider itself [RSELECT-015], [RSELECT-016].
On the full path, the router first lets that strategy router move the request to one of its tiers, another model name [RSELECT-061].

Figure strategy-choice: Gather strategy routers; none registered: Ordinary deployment selection; some found: Request tags match one? yes: That router takes it; no: A router tagged default? yes: That router takes it; no: Tag filtering on? no: First router takes it; yes: Every router has tags? no: First router takes it; yes: Ordinary deployments too? yes: Ordinary deployment selection; no: First router takes it; That router takes it, or First router takes it, by its own logic: Router's logic picks a tier
note: Fixed. The old single node is now three nodes in a chain, one per condition of RSELECT-108: 'tag filtering is on (router-wide `enable_tag_filtering`, or `request_kwargs["enable_tag_filtering"] is True`), every candidate carries tags, and at least one of the name's deployments is a plain (non-marker) deployment'. Only all three 'yes' answers reach 'Ordinary deployment selection'. Each 'no' goes to 'First router takes it', which matches RSELECT-109 ('Otherwise the first candidate is selected, so an untagged marker or a marker-only name captures untagged requests'). The round-4 counterexample (one untagged strategy router, tag filtering on, ordinary deployments present) now follows 'Every router has tags? no' to 'First router takes it'. sentence: Gather the strategy routers: The hook collects the strategy routers under the name from four kinds, in order: auto, complexity, adaptive and quality routers [RSELECT-105]. With none registered, no strategy router runs [RSELECT-105].

Tags choose the router, not the tier: A request with tags goes to the first strategy router whose tags match its own [RSELECT-106]. That router's own logic then picks the tier [RSELECT-098], [RSELECT-061].
Then the default tag: Otherwise the first strategy router tagged default takes the request [RSELECT-107].

Ordinary deployments keep unmatched traffic: Suppose no router matched so far, tag filtering is on, every strategy router under the name has tags, and the name also has ordinary deployments [RSELECT-108]. Then the request skips the strategy routers and goes to the ordinary deployments [RSELECT-108].

Otherwise the first router: Otherwise the first strategy router under the name takes the request [RSELECT-109]. So when one strategy router under the name has no tags, or the name has no ordinary deployments, requests that no tag rule placed still go to a strategy router [RSELECT-109].

The tier replaces the request: The chosen router's answer replaces the requested model and messages for the rest of selection, and the caller's own messages stay unchanged [RSELECT-061], [RSELECT-076].
A strategy router is a marker deployment whose provider model starts with `auto_router/` [RSELECT-015].
The pre-routing hook clears the previous attempt's routing decision, follows one alias hop, applies the session binding, runs any routing plugins, then chooses a strategy router [RSELECT-092].
With none chosen, it returns no response and selection goes on with the requested name [RSELECT-093].
The answer can carry tier params, such as an output-token limit or a reasoning effort, which overwrite same-named request settings [RSELECT-035], [RSELECT-034], [RSELECT-037].
Only provider-rejectable params outside the never-dropped set and any `allowed_openai_params` list can be dropped [RSELECT-031].
The router drops one only when no deployment of the target group accepts it, and an empty target group drops nothing [RSELECT-032], [RSELECT-033].
The session binding needs a `x-claude-code-session-id` header of at least 8 letters, digits, underscores or hyphens, plus an API key hash [RSELECT-110].
A request without `x-claude-code-agent-id` whose name selects a strategy binds the session to that name for 3600 seconds [RSELECT-116].

Requests with the agent id header then route through the bound router while it still selects a strategy for the caller, renewing the binding; otherwise the router deletes it [RSELECT-113]-[RSELECT-115].
Fallback hops, with `fallback_depth` set to anything but 0, skip the binding [RSELECT-112].
The router looks up the requested name by fixed rules and stops at the first rule that matches [RSELECT-020].
A generic fallback list can still serve a name that matches nothing [RSELECT-028].

A specific-deployment request: A request option can ask for deployments by provider model string, such as openai/gpt-4o, instead of by model name [RSELECT-021], [RSELECT-042]. The matches still pass the reservation filter, and an empty match is not an error during the lookup itself [RSELECT-021].

A deployment id: A name that is a deployment id, not a model name, returns that one deployment after the reservation filter [RSELECT-022]. From then on the router names it by its provider model, so an error about paused dep-0 names openai/gpt-4o [RSELECT-040], [RSELECT-042].
One alias hop: An alias renames the request exactly once [RSELECT-011].
Routing groups: A request that names a routing group gets every member's deployments as candidates [RSELECT-026], [RSETUP-093].
Unknown names: A name the router does not know tries the caller team's deployments under that name, or every team's for an admin without a team, then wildcard routes [RSELECT-018].
Nothing under the name: When the caller's team has no deployment under the name, the router looks for deployments whose provider model string equals the name [RSELECT-027], [RSELECT-017].

Access groups end the lookup: When the access-group filter empties the list, neither the provider-model match nor the generic fallback list runs, and the lookup fails with status 400 [RSELECT-027], [RSELECT-287], [RSELECT-288]. That error names no provider, so the configured fallbacks can still serve the request afterwards [FAILURE-113], [RDISP-101], [RDISP-111].
The generic fallback list: For a name that matches nothing, the lookup uses the first name of the first non-empty list under the star key, if that name is registered [RSELECT-028], [RSELECT-287].
Common resolution uses the name exactly as given, with no trimming, case folding or provider-prefix normalisation [RSELECT-220].
The access-group filter acts only when the caller's key lists allowed models that include one of the name's access groups but not the name itself, `"*"` or `"all-proxy-models"` [RSELECT-030].
The reservation filter drops strategy routers, applies access windows at the current UTC time, then provisioned-throughput shares [RSELECT-024].
Each raises `BadRequestError` when it withholds deployments and none survive, for example “Deployment gpt-4o is reserved for another team until 17:00 Europe/Berlin” [RSELECT-024].
A substitute from `fallbacks` resolves only as a registered name, never as an alias, routing group or wildcard route, and substitution never runs after an earlier rule returned [RSELECT-287].
When nothing remains, resolution raises `BadRequestError` (400) with an empty provider, naming the substitute if one was tried, else the requested name after its alias hop [RSELECT-288].
Because the error names no provider, the fallback dispatcher does not stop at it and can still walk the model's fallbacks [FAILURE-113], [RDISP-101].
After the lookup, a fixed chain of filters removes deployments that should not serve this request [RSELECT-040].
Filters never reorder deployments; only the final pick adds randomness or ranking [RSELECT-260].
Resolution comes first: The name that resolution returns replaces the requested name for every later step and error [RSELECT-040].

Team and web search: The team filter usually keeps deployments with no owner team plus the caller team's own [RSELECT-041], [TARGETS-100]. The web-search filter, for a request that asks for a web-search tool, keeps deployments not marked as lacking web search [RSELECT-041], [TARGETS-106], [TARGETS-107].

Only a deployment asked for by id skips the rest: A deployment asked for by id, or the default deployment, returns right after these two filters, or fails with a 503 (service unavailable) error when paused [RSELECT-042]. A model group with one deployment still goes through every filter, so its paused deployment ends in the 429 instead [RSELECT-042].
Health before cooldown: Health checks remove unhealthy deployments only when health-check routing is on, and they run before cooldowns [RSELECT-043], [RSELECT-142].

Resting deployments drop out: The cooldown filter removes deployments resting after recent errors [RSELECT-044]. If that empties the list while health-check routing and an allowed-failures policy are both set, the router logs a warning and keeps the resting deployments [RSELECT-045].
Callback checks: Optional extra checks follow, such as rate limits, affinity, prompt caching and stream continuation [RSELECT-047].
Pre-call checks need a switch: These checks run only when the router has them switched on and the request has messages or input [RSELECT-048].
Nothing left: An empty list ends in the no-deployment error, status 429 (too many requests), which here means no deployment could take the request [RSELECT-054], [RSELECT-283].
The 503 is `ServiceUnavailableError`, naming the provider model, not the id [RSELECT-042].
Health checks also do nothing when `allowed_fails_policy` is set without background health-check groups [RSELECT-142].

If every candidate is unhealthy, the full path keeps the whole list, but for a health-check probe the filter returns an empty list, and the call then ends in the no-deployment error [RSELECT-145], [RSELECT-054].
note: RSELECT-145: 'In the async health filter, when every candidate would be removed it returns an empty list if health_check_probe is true and the unfiltered list otherwise, without logging.' The sync twin (RSELECT-146) also keeps the list, with a warning, so 'the full path keeps the whole list' is not contradicted. RSELECT-054: 'When no candidate survives, the async pipeline ... raises the RouterRateLimitError'. An empty list from the health filter stays empty through the cooldown filter (its health-check-routing bypass restores the same empty list), the blocked filter, tag routing (it skips an empty list) and the order and exclusion filters, then hits the empty-list raise (router.py:14533-14546); the optional callback checks were not traced one by one. The only intervening raises are the routing-plugin ValueError (RSELECT-089) and the pre-call UnsupportedParamsError (RSELECT-208), which hit any empty list under those settings, and the story states the same general rule elsewhere ('An empty list ends in the no-deployment error'). The only probe caller, the complexity router, catches that error and treats the group as unavailable.

sentence: The paused filter counts only `model_info.blocked` equal to the value true, so the string `"true"` does not count [RSELECT-141].
Pre-call checks need `enable_pre_call_checks` on and messages or input in the request [RSELECT-048].
They exclude a deployment over its context window, at its per-minute request limit, or outside the requested region [RSELECT-202]-[RSELECT-204].
The per-minute check reads only this process's in-memory counts and skips entirely under a router-wide `usage-based-routing-v2` [RSELECT-203], [RSELECT-232], [RSELECT-251].
The order filter keeps the requested `_target_order`, or else the lowest declared `order`, or everything when no deployment declares one [RSELECT-051].
The router then removes the failover exclusion list even if that empties the list, but removes the retry skip list only when something would remain [RSELECT-052], [RSELECT-053].
When deployments survive, a strategy picks one, by default at random [RSELECT-067], [RSELECT-139].
When none survives, the caller usually gets a 429 error that names a wait time [RSELECT-054], [RSELECT-283].
0s, d0: starts a 60-second cooldown (resting)
10s, req: resolution finds both deployments (two candidates)
10s, req: cooldown filter drops dep-0 (one candidate)
10s, d1: the shuffle picks it (serving)
20s, d1: starts a 60-second cooldown (resting)
30s, req: cooldown filter drops both (empty list)
30s, req: error says retry in 60 seconds (429, all in cooldown)
60s, d0: cooldown length passes (serving again)
80s, d1: cooldown length passes (serving again)
Under `simple-shuffle` the pick is weighted random by each deployment's weight, rpm or tpm when set, else uniform [RSELECT-067].
Other strategies ask their selector, and a missing selector or an empty answer raises the no-deployment error [RSELECT-068].
A per-request strategy override that differs from the router-wide strategy adds one last check on every pick except a shuffle pick [RSELECT-284].
The no-deployment error is `RouterRateLimitError`, a `ValueError` subclass with status 429 [RSELECT-054].
Its message says no deployment is available for the model and gives a wait: the smallest configured cooldown length among the group's deployments, not the time remaining [RSELECT-283].
With no cooldown entry, or a smallest length of 0, the wait is the cooldown default fixed when the router was built, 5 seconds unless set [RSELECT-283], [RSELECT-282].
In the example each cooldown lasts 60 seconds, so the error at the 30s mark says 60 although dep-0 is halfway through its cooldown [RSELECT-283].
The message adds that all deployments are in cooldown only when every deployment id of the group is cooling, as here [RSELECT-283].
On the full path, the failure handlers receive the error when the request carries a logging object [RSELECT-071].
The whole asynchronous selection runs inside the selection trace `route <model>` [RSELECT-072].
The settings update changes some router settings while the router runs, and the next request uses them [RSELECT-252].
Other settings keep the values the router was built with, and the update leaves only a debug log line [RSELECT-152], [RSELECT-252].

Which keys count: The update applies the strategy and its settings, routing groups, aliases, fallback lists, retry counts, retry wait and retry policies, allowed failures, timeouts and cooldown time [RSELECT-152]. It also applies weighted failover, stream continuation, tag filtering and its prefix, optional checks and unsupported-parameter fallbacks [RSELECT-152].

Everything else is ignored: Any other key is dropped with only a debug log line, including pre-call checks, health-check routing, the allowed-failures policy, background health-check groups, tag match-any, routing plugins and default fallbacks [RSELECT-152], [RSELECT-252]. Those change only when code sets the router's own value or a new router is built [RSELECT-252].
Whole numbers only: Timeout, retry count, retry wait, allowed failures and cooldown time become whole numbers, so 2.9 becomes 2 and a timeout of 0.5 becomes 0 [RSELECT-153].
No rollback: Keys apply one at a time in the order given, so a bad value stops the update after the earlier keys took effect [RSELECT-153].
A new strategy rebuilds: A different strategy name rebuilds the strategy, and an unknown name fails before the setting changes [RSELECT-158], [RSELECT-159].
The settings update is `update_settings` [RSELECT-152].
`get_settings` returns live attribute values, not copies, with two exceptions [RSELECT-150].
Latency-based routing args come back as a new dict with defaults filled in, and routing groups as a list of dicts [RSELECT-151].
The cache flush, `flush_cache`, is a router method that `reset` also runs, not a setting [RSELECT-183], [RSELECT-184].
With Redis attached it issues `FLUSHALL`, which erases every key on that Redis server [RSELECT-183], [RSELECT-274].

Asking for a deployment by its id skips health checks, cooldowns and pre-call checks, so a deployment resting after errors still gets the request [RSELECT-042]. An access window or a provisioned-throughput share still applies, and a paused deployment still gives a 503 [RSELECT-022], [RSELECT-042].

Only the router-wide strategy decides the path [RSELECT-060]. Under one such as usage-based-routing, asynchronous calls skip the strategy routers, team filter, affinity and rate-limit checks, whatever strategy its routing group names [RSELECT-278], [RSELECT-128].

The strategy name provider-budget-routing passes validation but sets up no way to choose a deployment, which looks like a defect [RSELECT-279]. For a model outside any routing group every request then fails, even with one deployment; only a request by deployment id still works [RSELECT-279].
Flushing the router's cache erases every key on its shared Redis server, including other applications' data [RSELECT-274], [RSELECT-183].

The wait in the no-deployment error is the configured cooldown length, not the time left [RSELECT-283]. When no deployment of the group has a cooldown entry, as when all are paused, the error shows the build-time cooldown default, even after the cooldown time was changed [RSELECT-283], [RSELECT-282].
Setting the router-wide timeout to 0.5 seconds through the settings update stores 0, which calls then skip as unset, so the half-second limit is lost [RSELECT-153], [RSELECT-275], [RCALL-083].

A routing plugin's narrowed list of provider models stays on the request [RSELECT-276]. So a fallback to another model whose own plugin pass narrows nothing can fail with no deployments left after routing-plugin filtering [RSELECT-276], [RSELECT-089].

When filters leave no deployment, the full path writes an info log line, and the reduced path writes none [RSELECT-054], [RSELECT-126]. The reduced path calls no failure handlers [RSELECT-128]. An asynchronous call handed to it still runs inside the selection trace; a synchronous call gets no trace from selection [RSELECT-072], [RSELECT-128]. On every path the error reaches the caller's retry and fallback loop, which logs an error line when a fallback walk fails [RSELECT-225], [RDISP-114].
note: Fixed. The no-log-line rule is now limited to the filters case, as RSELECT-126 says: 'An empty candidate list raises, without a log line, the `RouterRateLimitError`'. The code agrees: router.py:15732-15755 raises right after the last filter with no logger call. The info line of RSELECT-127 (a missing selector or a `None` pick, which includes provider-budget-routing per RSELECT-279) belongs to the strategy pick, not the filters, so it no longer conflicts. The story's own sections keep filters and the strategy pick apart. The failure-handler sentence is now on its own. RSELECT-128 lists 'the failure-handler dispatch' among the steps sync selection skips, and the async hand-off at router.py:14700-14713 sits outside the try block that dispatches them (14830-14844). The trace and retry-loop sentences are unchanged: RSELECT-072, RSELECT-128, RSELECT-225 and RDISP-114. Too fine for this bullet: the health and cooldown bypass warnings (router.py:15687, router.py:16104) fire only when a filter would empty the list and is skipped, on both paths.
